title: Support networks aim to help kids through the polycrisis
gist: Youth-focused emotional-support networks like Force of Nature and the Good Grief Network's GGN-Z have scaled to thousands of participants to help young people cope with 'polycrisis' anxiety (climate plus geopolitics, cost of living, AI job fears), but a persistent research gap means almost none of these programs have published evidence that they actually work.

insights.claim: A 2021 landmark study in The Lancet Planetary Health surveying 10,000 children and young people across 10 countries found about 60% were very or extremely worried about climate change, more than 45% said eco-anxiety affected their daily ability to function, and 56% agreed with the statement 'Humanity is doomed.'
insights.speaker: Sarah Scoles
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of youth climate distress as a mainstream, near-majority phenomenon rather than a fringe concern -- relevant for sizing demand for mental-health and youth-support interventions.
insights.quote: 56% of the young respondents nevertheless agreed with the statement “Humanity is doomed.”
insights.locator: In 2021, researchers published a landmark study

insights.claim: A 2025 Polish study defining a 'polycrisis syndrome' found more than 60% of surveyed young people reported psychological difficulties -- emotional-regulation problems, depression symptoms, and lower overall well-being -- attributed to the cumulative stress of world affairs broadly, not climate alone.
insights.speaker: Sarah Scoles
insights.so_what: Shows the distress driver has broadened beyond climate to a compound set of stressors (conflict, cost of living, AI job anxiety), which should reshape how support programs and researchers frame the problem.
insights.quote: more than 60% reported problems —difficulty regulating emotion, symptoms of depression, and lower overall mental and physical well-being—that they attributed to the cumulative stress of world affairs

insights.claim: In an early-1980s Cold War-era survey of 130 US high schools, about 35% of seniors agreed nuclear or biological annihilation would probably end humanity within their lifetime, and a Gallup poll found 49% of teens said fear of nuclear war shaped their future planning -- yet a majority still agreed humanity had come through tough times before, a more optimistic baseline than seen in current youth surveys.
insights.speaker: Sarah Scoles
insights.so_what: Provides a historical baseline showing today's youth distress may be comparable in intensity to Cold War-era fear but notably lacking the accompanying optimism the earlier generation retained.
insights.quote: Nuclear or biological annihilation will probably be the fate of all mankind within my lifetime
insights.locator: In the early 1980s, during the latter years of the Cold War

insights.claim: Psychotherapist Caroline Hickman, who led the Lancet Planetary Health study, argues that youth distress is not only about planetary decline but is fundamentally anger that adults and institutions -- faith leaders, school leaders, government officials -- broke an implicit social contract to protect their future.
insights.speaker: Sarah Scoles
insights.so_what: Reframes youth eco-anxiety as an institutional-trust crisis rather than purely an environmental one, implying interventions that only address climate literacy may miss the underlying grievance.
insights.quote: and that social contract was being broken repeatedly.
insights.locator: Caroline Hickman, the psychotherapist who led the Lancet Planetary Health study

themes.theme: Support Networks Scaling Fast, Broadening Scope

insights.claim: Force of Nature, founded in 2019 by then-teenager Clover Hogan, ran its free 'Becoming a Force of Nature' Zoom program for about 900 participants last year and now has roughly 2,000 students from more than 50 countries in its online community.
insights.speaker: Sarah Scoles
insights.so_what: Provides concrete scale metrics (900 annual program participants, 2,000-strong community across 50+ countries) for benchmarking growth of youth climate-support organizations.
insights.quote: Force of Nature had around 900 participants in Becoming a Force of Nature last year and has about 2,000 students from more than 50 countries in its online community.
insights.locator: Force of Nature had around 900 participants

insights.claim: Force of Nature deliberately broadened its messaging beyond climate-specific language because privileged-country youth experience mostly philosophical eco-anxiety while others are in acute 'survival mode' responding to immediate crises, and single-issue climate framing was limiting the program to an echo chamber.
insights.speaker: Sarah Scoles
insights.so_what: Suggests that youth mental-health programs positioned around a single crisis (climate) may face a structural ceiling on reach compared with those addressing the broader polycrisis.
insights.locator: They made the shift, Hooper says, for two reasons

insights.claim: The Good Grief Network's adult 10-step program, modeled on Alcoholics Anonymous, has run more than 85 times with about 2,500 total participants; its teen spinoff GGN-Z is a condensed 5-step, experiential program that has been piloted since 2022 with kids in Northern California and remains small.
insights.speaker: Sarah Scoles
insights.so_what: Establishes the current scale ceiling (2,500 adult participants over years of operation) for AA-model emotional-support interventions in this space, useful for sizing the category.
insights.locator: Igras and a collaborator began testing it in 2022

insights.claim: The Good Grief Network claims 90% of its participants report feeling more empowered and less alone, but has not published any underlying data or methodology to support that figure -- illustrative of a broader evidence gap across youth eco-anxiety interventions.
insights.speaker: Sarah Scoles
insights.so_what: A headline efficacy statistic with no published backing is a red flag for anyone evaluating which youth-support programs deserve funding or scaling.
insights.quote: GGN said 90% of participants in its programs felt more empowered and less alone, it didn’t publish any data or methods backing up that finding
insights.locator: The team included the Good Grief Network

insights.claim: A 2021 scoping review by psychologist Liza Jachens found 34 existing eco-anxiety programs, of which only two had conducted any formal self-evaluation; a follow-up 2024 review led by Siqi Xue of the University of Toronto found the evidence gap had not closed.
insights.speaker: Sarah Scoles
insights.so_what: Quantifies just how immature the evidence base is across the whole eco-anxiety intervention field (2 of 34 programs formally evaluated) -- a clear underinvestment relative to program count.
insights.quote: She found 34 in existence. Of those, only two had done any formal evaluation on themselves.
insights.locator: Jachens, for instance, coauthored a 2021 scoping review

insights.claim: Force of Nature has joined a 25-organization, five-year research initiative called 'Youth Mental Wellbeing' intended to build a comparative evidence base showing which youth polycrisis interventions actually work.
insights.speaker: Sarah Scoles
insights.so_what: A coordinated, multi-year, cross-organization evaluation effort is a concrete signal that the field is moving toward the evidence standards it currently lacks.
insights.locator: Force of Nature is also trying to quantify its impact

insights.claim: Scholar Panu Pihkala's 'coping model' -- express emotions, learn to regulate them, take action, form meaning, and practice self-care and healthy distance from big feelings -- underlies Sweden's Climate Emotion School curriculum and is emerging as a template other programs are adopting.
insights.speaker: Sarah Scoles
insights.so_what: Provides a named, citable intervention framework that investors or funders evaluating youth mental-health programs could use as a quality benchmark.
insights.locator: Its curriculum was shaped by the work of Panu Pihkala

insights.claim: Psychologist Liza Jachens finds that validation and connection precede action-taking -- people who feel genuinely heard in their distress move naturally toward wanting to do something -- suggesting emotional-support infrastructure is a precondition for, not a substitute for, youth civic engagement.
insights.speaker: Sarah Scoles
insights.so_what: Implies programs should sequence emotional validation before activism/action components to be effective, a design principle relevant to any organization building youth engagement products.
insights.quote: When people feel genuinely heard and held in their distress, they tend to move quite naturally toward wanting to do something.
insights.locator: these analyses do have bright spots
